tier_reason: The benchmark_url mirror has the SIGMOD 2021 abstract verbatim: 2x faster inserts than the Morton filter, lookup and delete performance similar to the cuckoo filter, and 3x insert scaling with 4 threads. That is a peer-reviewed win over the named baseline. It is not A: the full paper (the source for CPU and compiler) returned 403 from both curl and WebFetch, and the repo's own src/bm.cc benchmarks only the VQF, with no Morton, cuckoo or quotient comparison code.

corrections.caveats: The headline 2x speed claim is against the Morton filter, not directly against Bloom, cuckoo or xor filters. Against the cuckoo filter itself, the paper claims only parity ('similar lookup and deletion performance'), not a win. The paper's CPU model, compiler and flags could not be checked: the paper is gold open access (CC-BY) at dl.acm.org, but it returned HTTP 403 to curl and WebFetch, and the abstract was confirmed through a GitHub-hosted paper-index mirror. The repo Makefile builds with gcc/g++ -Ofast -march=native -msse4.2 and uses AVX-512 when lscpu reports avx512bw, with an AVX2 fallback. The repo holds no baseline-comparison harness.

notes: All claim numbers match the abstract. The last commit on the default branch (master) is 2024-05-19; the record's 2024-07-16 is the repo's pushed_at, and no branch has a later commit. The status stays 'stale'. BSD-3-Clause, 13 stars, not archived and not a fork, all confirmed through gh.

tier_reason: The README 'Performance comparisons' section shows first-party, single-run CLI output for binaryfuse8 against bloom12 over 10M HIBP hashes. The code is public (src/build_filter.cpp, src/query_filter.cpp, built with -O3), but the page gives no CPU model and no compiler for the run. That makes it C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Construction: 0.420s vs 0.613s for bloom12 (~1.46x faster, derived from page data). Serialized size: 11,272,228 vs 15,000,024 bytes (~1.33x smaller, derived from page data). Single-query processing time: 241 µs vs 344 µs, which the tool reports as 4149.377 vs 2906.977 expected queries/sec (~1.43x, derived from page data). All figures come from one-off runs.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The Makefile builds with 'c++ -O3 -std=c++11'. The compiler and version used for the README run are not stated; CI runs GCC 11 on Ubuntu 22.04, but that is only a sanitized build/test job, not the benchmark run.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are single-run wall-clock output copied from example README commands, not repeated or averaged, and the CPU model is not stated. The query comparison is one query per filter, and those times likely include memory-mapping and page-fault costs. The two example queries also gave different answers for the same key: binaryfuse8 printed 'Surely not in the set' and bloom12 printed 'Probably in the set', so the single-query times are not like-for-like. The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub license API returns 404). The README says the reusable library is FastFilter/xor_singleheader.

notes: Every number in the claim is on the README. The only fixes are marking the ratios as derived from page data and correcting compiler_and_flags, since the CI badge does not describe the benchmark machine. No license, so 'reference' is correct. The last commit is 2024-12-09 and 50 stars is correct.

tier_reason: The README Performance section has first-party BenchmarkDotNet time ratios from one run on .NET 10 x64, and the benchmark code is public (src/BinaryFuseFilter.Benchmarks/QueryBenchmarks.cs, ConstructionBenchmarks.cs). The page does not state the CPU model, so it is C.

corrections.caveats: This is a very new, single-author repo (1 star; the NuGet package BinaryFuseFilter 1.0.0 has about 131 total downloads). The CPU model is not stated, so the evidence is capped below A/B. The comparison is not like-for-like: per QueryBenchmarks.cs, BinaryFuse8Filter queries pre-hashed ulong keys, while BloomFilter.NetCore and XORFilterDotNet receive 8-byte arrays and hash them internally (the source notes this for XORFilterDotNet). Part of the 20.76x query ratio is therefore hashing overhead and BloomFilter.NetCore's implementation, not a fundamental Bloom-filter limit. All figures are ratios from a single run; no absolute times are published.

notes: The README tables match the claim exactly. Query ratios: Bloom 20.76, XOR 8.68. Construction ratios: Bloom 2.32 time / 86 allocation; XOR 58.6 time / 366 allocation. MIT, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-03 ('active'), all confirmed through gh.
